source_text:
ἄρα ὁ τῷ κόκκῳ δεδωκὼς τὴν σπερματικὴν δύναμιν, ἔδωκε καὶ τοῖς ἡμετέροις
σώμασι τὴν τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἰσχύν. Οὐχ ὡς ὅμοιον τῷ τῶν καρπῶν καὶ τῶν
ἀνθρώπων παρέλαβον σῶμα, ἀλλ' ἵνα τὴν δημιουργικὴν δύναμιν παραστήσω. 1 Kor
15,40–42 Οὐχ ὡς ἀνισταμένων τῶν ἄλλων σαρκῶν· ὑποδείγματι γὰρ κέχρηται. καὶ
σώματα ἐπουράνια τὸν ἥλιον λέγει καὶ τὴν σελήνην, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς δείκνυσιν. οὕτως
καὶ ἡ ἀνάστασις τῶν νεκρῶν. ὁρᾷς ὅτι ὑπόδειγμα ἦν τὰ πρῶτα· ἀποδέδοται δὲ νῦν οὗ
ἐστι τὸ ὑπόδειγμα. Σώματα δὲ οὐράνια ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη. 1 Kor 15,44 Σῶμα ψυχικὸν
λέγει τὸ τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς θανατωθέν, πνευματικὸν δὲ τὸ τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ
πνεύματος ἐγειρόμενον, ὅπερ οὐκέτι κατὰ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀσθένειαν ζήσεται ἥτις οὐκ
ἐξαρκεῖ φυλάττειν τὴν τοῦ σώματος σύστασιν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ πνεύματος
δύναμιν ἥτις εἰς ἀθανασίαν αὐτὸ μεθίστησιν. 276 1 Kor 15,45 Τοῦτο Μωϋσῆς φησι τὸ
καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος εἰς πνεῦμα
ζωοποιοῦν. τοῦτο τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον λέγει· τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν
ἁγίου. 1 Kor 15,47 Ἐκ γῆς ὁ ἄνθρωπος κατὰ φύσιν, χοϊκὸς δὲ κατὰ τὴν προαίρεσιν. ἐξ
οὐρανοῦ δὲ τὸν Χριστὸν λέγει· οὐ καθ' ὁμοιότητα ἢ ἐξ ἀναστάσεως ἀϊδιότης γίνεται.
1 Kor 15,47–49 Ἐπιτρέχουσι τούτῳ καὶ οἱ περὶ Οὐαλεντῖνον καὶ Μαρκίωνα καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ
Φωτεινοῦ καὶ οἱ Ἀπολιναρίου, πάντας δὲ ἐλέγχει τὸ ῥητόν. ἐρωτῶ γάρ· ὁ ἐκ γῆς
χοϊκὸς εἶχεν ψυχὴν ἢ οὔ; οὐκ ἀρνήσονται. καὶ ὁ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κύριος εἶχεν σῶμα ἀπὸ
γῆς. πάλιν ἐρωτῶ· διὰ τί τὸν μὲν πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον ἐκ γῆς χοϊκὸν λέγει, τὸν δὲ
κύριον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ; μετὰ ταῦτα· οἷος ὁ χοϊκός–καὶ οὐκέτι γῆς μέμνηται ἀλλ' ὅτι–
τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ χοϊκοί; ἢ δηλονότι ἐπειδὴ τὸ μὲν ἐκ γῆς τῆς φύσεως, τὸ δὲ χοϊκὸς τῆς
προαιρέσεως. ἐλθὼν εἰς τὸ οἷος ὁ χοϊκός, καὶ κατηγορῶν τῶν οὐ καλῶς βιωσάντων,
οὐκέτι τῆς φύσεως μνημονεύει οὐδὲ τοῦ ἐκ γῆς, καὶ τὸν κύριον οὐκέτι ἐξ οὐρανοῦ
λέγει ἀλλ' ἐπουράνιον· πάλιν ἦσαν ἐκ γῆς καὶ οἱ πνευματικοί. οἷος δὲ ὁ χοϊκός,
τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ χοϊκοί, καὶ οἷος ὁ ἐπουράνιος τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ ἐπουράνιοι. καὶ πᾶσα
ἀνάγκη, εἰ ἀρνοῖντό τινες τὸ σάρκα ἀνειληφέναι τὸν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κύριον, ἐπειδὴ ἐξ
οὐρανοῦ καὶ τοὺς ἐπουρανίους, μὴ συγχωρεῖν ἀνειληφέναι σῶμα, ἐπειδὴ οἷος ὁ
χοϊκός, τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ χοϊκοί, καὶ οὕτως οὐδαμόθεν ἵσταται τοῦτο νοούμενον
pass_a_gloss: [15:35-38 note, continued] So the one who has given to the grain the seminal power has given also to our bodies the strength of the resurrection. Not as similar did I take up the body of the crops and of men, but so that I may present the creative power. [Label 1 Kor 15,40-42] Not as of the other fleshes rising; for he has used an illustration. And he calls heavenly bodies the sun and the moon, and the following shows [it]: so also the resurrection of the dead. You see that the first things were an illustration; and now that of which the illustration is has been given. [Repeat, not printed again: And heavenly bodies, sun and moon.] [Label 1 Kor 15,44] He calls soul-body the one put to death by the sin of the soul, and spiritual the one raised by the power of the Spirit, which will no longer live according to the weakness of the soul, which does not suffice to guard the constitution of the body, but according to the power of the Spirit, which transfers it into immortality. [Page 276; label 1 Kor 15,45] This Moses says: 'and the man became a living soul.' The second man into a life-giving spirit. This the Gospel says: 'for the thing begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit.' [Label 1 Kor 15,47] The man [is] from earth according to nature, but earthy according to choice. And he says Christ [is] from heaven: not according to likeness or from resurrection does eternity come about. [Label 1 Kor 15,47-49] Both those around Valentinus and Marcion and those from Photinus and those of Apollinarius run to this, but the saying refutes all. For I ask: did the earthy one from earth have a soul or not? They will not deny. And the Lord from heaven had a body from earth. Again I ask: why does he call the first man from earth earthy, but the Lord from heaven? After these: 'such as the earthy' (and he no longer mentions earth but that) 'such also the earthy ones'? Or clearly since the 'from earth' [is] of nature, and the 'earthy' of choice. Having come to 'such as the earthy', and accusing those who did not live well, he no longer mentions nature nor the 'from earth', and he no longer calls the Lord from heaven but heavenly; again, the spiritual too were from earth. 'Such as the earthy, such also the earthy ones, and such as the heavenly, such also the heavenly ones.' And every necessity, if some should deny that the Lord from heaven has taken up flesh, since from heaven, [then] also [as to] the heavenly ones not to grant that they have taken up a body, since 'such as the earthy, such also the earthy ones', and so from nowhere does this stand, being understood... [continues]
pass_b_english: So he who gave the grain its power as seed has also given our bodies the strength to rise. I did not bring in the body of crops and of men as though they were alike, but to set before you the Creator's power.

On 1 Corinthians 15:40–42: Not as though the other kinds of flesh rise; he is using an illustration. By “heavenly bodies” he means the sun and the moon, and what follows shows it: “So also is the resurrection of the dead.” You see that what came first was an illustration; now he has given the thing the illustration was for.

On 1 Corinthians 15:44: By the body “of the soul” he means the body put to death by the soul's sin, and by the “spiritual” body the one raised by the power of the Spirit. That body will no longer live by the weakness of the soul, which is not strong enough to hold the body's frame together, but by the power of the Spirit, which carries it over into immortality.

On 1 Corinthians 15:45: This is what Moses says: “And the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). The second man became a life-giving spirit. This is what the Gospel says: “For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20).
On 1 Corinthians 15:47: Man is “from the earth” by nature, and “earthy” by choice. He says that Christ is “from heaven”: not by likeness; nor does eternity come from resurrection.

On 1 Corinthians 15:47–49: The followers of Valentinus and Marcion, the followers of Photinus and those of Apollinarius all run to this text, but the passage refutes them all. I ask: did the earthy man from the earth have a soul or not? They will not deny it. And the Lord from heaven had a body from the earth. Again I ask: why does he call the first man “from the earth, earthy,” but the Lord “from heaven”? And after that, “As is the earthy” (and he no longer mentions earth, but says) “so are those who are earthy”? Clearly because “from the earth” belongs to nature, while “earthy” belongs to choice. When he comes to “as is the earthy,” and is accusing those who have not lived well, he no longer mentions nature or “from the earth,” and he no longer calls the Lord “from heaven” but “heavenly.” Again, the spiritual too were from the earth. “As is the earthy, so are those who are earthy, and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.” And it follows of necessity: if some deny that the Lord from heaven took flesh, because he is from heaven, they must also refuse to grant that the heavenly ones took a body, since “as is the earthy, so are those who are earthy.” And so this stands on no ground at all if it is understood…

choices.why: Severianus's gloss turns on ψυχή (the soul's sin, the soul's weakness); 'natural' would hide it.

choices.english: “from the earth” by nature, “earthy” by choice
choices.why: Severianus's distinction drives the whole 15:47-49 note.
